title: A Fully Discrete Local Discontinuous Galerkin Method for Quasilinear Stochastic Convection-Diffusion-Type Equations
summary: In this paper, we develop and analyze a fully discrete local discontinuous Galerkin (LDG) method with IMEX-Euler time discretization for a class of multi-dimensional quasilinear stochastic convection-diffusion-type equations driven by multiplicative $\mathcal Q$-Wiener noise. The leading diffusion matrix may depend on the solution as well as the spatial and temporal variables, while the lower-order drift and noise coefficients may depend on both the solution and its gradient. Under a suitable stochastic parabolicity condition, we establish unconditional high-moment stability estimates for the fully discrete scheme in the quasilinear setting. In the semilinear setting, where the leading diffusion matrix is independent of the solution but may vary in space and time, we further prove optimal high-moment strong error estimates of order $\mathcal O(h^{r+1})$ in space and $\mathcal O(k^{1/2})$ in time. A pathwise error estimate is then derived by combining the high-moment error bound with a discrete Kolmogorov argument. Numerical experiments are presented to illustrate the stability and convergence properties of the proposed method.

AI.tldr: A fully discrete LDG method with IMEX-Euler time discretization is developed and analyzed for multi-dimensional quasilinear stochastic convection-diffusion equations with multiplicative Q-Wiener noise, proving unconditional high-moment stability and optimal strong error estimates.
AI.motivation: Quasilinear stochastic convection-diffusion-type equations driven by multiplicative Q-Wiener noise lack rigorous numerical analysis, particularly fully discrete schemes with provable stability and high-moment convergence in the quasilinear setting.
AI.method: Local discontinuous Galerkin (LDG) spatial discretization combined with IMEX-Euler time stepping, using a stochastic parabolicity condition to handle solution-dependent leading diffusion and gradient-dependent drift/noise coefficients.
AI.result: Unconditional high-moment stability for the fully discrete scheme in the quasilinear setting; in the semilinear setting, optimal high-moment strong error estimates of O(h^{r+1}) in space and O(k^{1/2}) in time, plus a pathwise error estimate via a discrete Kolmogorov argument. Numerical experiments confirm stability and convergence.
AI.conclusion: The proposed LDG-IMEX-Euler scheme is stable and optimally convergent for quasilinear stochastic convection-diffusion equations, with pathwise error control, validated by numerical experiments.

title: Global Sensitivity Analysis of Spatial Sets: Finite-Element-Based Estimation and the Role of Observation Windows
summary: In this work we consider numerical models with random input parameters, where the model output is a spatially distributed random field. We carry out a statistical sensitivity analysis of spatial sets which arise for instance when the model output exceeds a critical threshold. We consider two approaches: (i) a kernel-based sensitivity analysis working with the Hilbert--Schmidt Independence Criterion, and (ii) a function-valued sensitivity analysis working with generalized Sobol' indices, where the model output is the indicator function of the spatial set of interest. We develop efficient estimators for the sensitivity indices, especially for finite-element-based numerical models, where we approximate volume integrals in the sensitivity measures by finite element quadrature, thereby avoiding Monte Carlo sampling over the spatial domain. This improves the state-of-the-art for the kernel-based indices and makes these methods practically accessible for expensive numerical models. For the generalized Sobol' indices we utilize the same finite element quadrature for efficient computation. We present numerical experiments for a hydrogen combustion process, modeled by a coupled system of convection-diffusion-reaction equations in a two-dimensional spatial domain, and ask whether the temperature remains below a critical value in selected regions of the combustion domain. Our results show that in this example the kernel-based and the generalized Sobol' indices give qualitatively similar input importance rankings. Moreover, the ranking depends on the chosen observation window and can flip between different windows. The algorithms for implementing the proposed methods are provided in the supplementary materials and in an open source code repository.

AI.tldr: This paper performs statistical sensitivity analysis of spatial sets (e.g., where model output exceeds a threshold) using kernel-based Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion and function-valued generalized Sobol' indices, with efficient finite element quadrature estimators.
AI.motivation: Numerical models with random inputs often produce spatially distributed outputs; analyzing sensitivity of spatial sets (threshold exceedance regions) is important but computationally challenging for expensive models.
AI.method: Two approaches: kernel-based sensitivity analysis via Hilbert-Schmidt Independence Criterion, and function-valued sensitivity analysis via generalized Sobol' indices using the indicator function of the spatial set. Efficient estimators approximate volume integrals by finite element quadrature, avoiding Monte Carlo sampling over the spatial domain.
AI.result: Applied to a hydrogen combustion process (coupled convection-diffusion-reaction equations in 2D), asking if temperature stays below a critical value. Kernel-based and generalized Sobol' indices give qualitatively similar rankings, which depend on the observation window and can flip between windows.
AI.conclusion: The finite element quadrature approach improves the state-of-the-art for kernel-based indices and makes them practical for expensive models; input importance rankings are window-dependent. Algorithms are available in supplementary materials and open source repository.

title: Transform before linearizing: robust Newton methods for singular $p$-Laplace and $p$-Stokes equations
summary: For $1<p<2$, the $p$-Laplace equation and its $p$-Stokes generalization are difficult to solve numerically. Newton's method converges rapidly only close to the solution, with iteration counts that grow under mesh refinement and deteriorate as $p\to1$. The more robust Picard iteration converges only linearly. Rather than globalizing or preconditioning Newton's method, we modify the system to which it is applied. We \emph{lift} the equation by introducing the flux $|\nabla u|^{p-2}\nabla u$ as an auxiliary (or ''lifting'') variable, apply a nonlinear \emph{transformation} to the resulting constitutive relation, \emph{linearize}, and \emph{eliminate} the auxiliary variable by static condensation. Lifting alone leaves the linearization unchanged; it is the preceding transformation that yields the new method. The elimination is algebraic and pointwise at the quadrature points, so the flux variable is never discretized, no inf-sup condition or indefinite system arises, and the cost per iteration is that of a standard Newton step. Together with a pointwise feasibility bound on the lifting variable that keeps the diffusion tensor uniformly positive definite, this yields an iteration that we prove, in finite dimensions and for the $p$-Laplace equation, to converge globally and locally at a quadratic rate; a one-dimensional model problem explains why the lagged flux variable removes the zig-zag behavior of standard Newton for $p$ close to one. Firedrake-based experiments for $p$-Laplace problems in two and three dimensions and for stationary and time-dependent $p$-Stokes flows show iteration counts largely insensitive to $p$ and to mesh refinement, and up to an order of magnitude fewer iterations than standard Newton for $p$ close to one.

AI.tldr: A lifted-transformed-linearized-eliminated (LTLE) variant of Newton's method for the p-Laplace and p-Stokes equations achieves global convergence, local quadratic rate, and iteration counts largely insensitive to p and mesh refinement.
AI.motivation: For 1<p<2, the p-Laplace equation and its p-Stokes generalization are hard to solve numerically: Newton's method converges fast only near the solution, with iteration counts that grow under mesh refinement and deteriorate as p→1, while more robust Picard iteration converges only linearly. The goal is a method that is both robust and fast without resorting to globalization or preconditioning of Newton.
AI.method: Instead of modifying Newton (globalization/preconditioning), the system is modified: lift the equation by introducing the flux |∇u|^{p-2}∇u as an auxiliary variable, apply a nonlinear transformation to the constitutive relation, linearize, and eliminate the auxiliary variable by static condensation. Lifting alone leaves the linearization unchanged; the transformation yields the new method. Elimination is algebraic and pointwise at quadrature points, so the flux is never discretized (no inf-sup condition, no indefinite system), and per-iteration cost equals a standard Newton step. A pointwise feasibility bound on the lifting variable keeps the diffusion tensor uniformly positive definite.
AI.result: Proved global convergence and local quadratic rate in finite dimensions for the p-Laplace equation. A 1D model explains why the lagged flux variable removes standard Newton's zig-zag behavior for p close to 1. Firedrake experiments for p-Laplace in 2D/3D and for stationary/time-dependent p-Stokes show iteration counts largely insensitive to p and mesh refinement, and up to an order of magnitude fewer iterations than standard Newton for p close to 1.
AI.conclusion: Reformulating rather than preconditioning the system yields a globally convergent, locally quadratically convergent solver for p-Laplace/p-Stokes that is robust across p and mesh refinement, with Newton-like cost per iteration and no auxiliary discretization or inf-sup issues.

title: Error bounds for the Sherman-Morrison formula and its modification with improved stability
summary: It is known that the Sherman--Morrison (SM) formula is not numerically stable. In recent work, we introduced SMIR, an algorithm that incorporates iterative refinement to enhance the SM backward error. In this paper we take a different route: adapting an algorithm of Govaerts, originally designed for general bordered linear systems, we develop a modified Sherman--Morrison (MSM) method whose built-in self-correction makes it surprisingly resilient. Whereas standard SM requires the solution of two $n\times n$ linear systems, MSM requires three; by contrast, SMIR requires $2+k$ solves, where $k$ is the number of IR steps and can be substantially larger than three, when IR converges slowly. We then derive backward and forward error bounds for both SM and MSM. The SM backward error bound established here is stronger than the one proved in [Hashemi \& Nakatsukasa 2026]: it accounts for every rounding error and holds with no conditions on the size of the capacitance. From these bounds we extract growth factors that are cheap to compute a posteriori and can be used to certify the backward and forward stability of SM and MSM on a given problem. In our experiments, MSM consistently produces backward stable solutions, and is therefore observed to be forward stable as well. A formal proof of the stability --- or instability --- of MSM remains an open problem.

AI.tldr: The paper develops a modified Sherman–Morrison (MSM) method based on Govaerts' algorithm for bordered linear systems, whose built-in self-correction makes it numerically resilient. Error bounds and cheap a posteriori growth factors are derived to certify backward/forward stability of SM and MSM.
AI.motivation: The standard Sherman–Morrison (SM) formula is not numerically stable. Existing fixes like SMIR (iterative refinement) require many solves (2+k) and can converge slowly, so a more efficient and robust alternative is needed.
AI.method: Adapting Govaerts' algorithm for general bordered linear systems, the authors build MSM with built-in self-correction. MSM needs three n×n solves versus two for SM. They derive backward and forward error bounds for both SM and MSM, extracting a posteriori computable growth factors for stability certification.
AI.result: The new SM backward error bound is stronger than Hashemi & Nakatsukasa (2026), accounting for every rounding error with no conditions on capacitance size. Experiments show MSM consistently yields backward stable solutions and is observed forward stable, while formal proof remains open.
AI.conclusion: MSM offers a practical, resilient alternative to SM and SMIR, with cheap a posteriori certification of stability. However, formal proof of MSM's stability (or instability) is still an open problem.

title: Physics Based Triple Debye Dielectric Modeling and Multi Layer ADE FDTD Simulation of Terahertz Pulse Reflection for Breast Cancer Detection
summary: Terahertz (THz) imaging has emerged as a promising non-ionizing modality for breast cancer assessment owing to its intrinsic sensitivity to tissue hydration. However, existing dielectric descriptions of biological tissue, largely restricted to single- or double-Debye models, fail to capture the multiscale relaxation dynamics governing broadband THz dispersion and absorption, thereby limiting the quantitative interpretation of reflected pulse signatures.Here, a physics based triple Debye dielectric framework is developed to quantitatively predict broadband THz-tissue interactions. The proposed model explicitly incorporates three physically distinct relaxation processes associated with free-water rotational dynamics, bound-water relaxation (τ_2), and ultrafast interfacial/macromolecular polarization (τ_3). Model parameters are obtained by nonlinear least-squares fitting to experimentally measured refractive-index data digitized from published THz time-domain spectroscopy measurements of ex vivo human breast tissue. Compared with conventional Debye formulations, the proposed model substantially improves the fitting accuracy, reducing the root-mean-square error from 0.7773 (single Debye) and 0.2976 (double Debye) to only 0.0199 for the triple-Debye model. Fullwave FDTD ADE simulations of realistic multilayer breast structures further demonstrate that reflected THz pulses encode tissue hydration through reproducible temporal signatures, including increased reflection amplitude, delayed pulse arrival, and enhanced waveform broadening in malignant tissue. Polarization and angle resolved Fresnel analysis further indicates that hydration-dependent pseudo-Brewster minima provide an additional contrast mechanism by selectively suppressing reflections from low hydration normal and adipose tissues.

AI.tldr: A triple-Debye dielectric framework is developed to model broadband THz-tissue interactions in breast cancer imaging, dramatically improving fitting accuracy and revealing hydration-based contrast mechanisms in reflected pulse signatures.
AI.motivation: THz imaging is a promising non-ionizing modality for breast cancer assessment due to sensitivity to tissue hydration. However, existing dielectric descriptions (single- or double-Debye models) fail to capture the multiscale relaxation dynamics governing broadband THz dispersion and absorption, limiting quantitative interpretation of reflected pulse signatures.
AI.method: A physics-based triple-Debye dielectric framework is developed, incorporating three physically distinct relaxation processes: free-water rotational dynamics (τ_1), bound-water relaxation (τ_2), and ultrafast interfacial/macromolecular polarization (τ_3). Model parameters are obtained via nonlinear least-squares fitting to refractive-index data from published THz time-domain spectroscopy of ex vivo human breast tissue. Full-wave FDTD ADE simulations of multilayer breast structures and polarization/angle-resolved Fresnel analysis are also performed.
AI.result: The triple-Debye model reduces RMSE from 0.7773 (single Debye) and 0.2976 (double Debye) to 0.0199. FDTD simulations show reflected THz pulses encode tissue hydration via reproducible temporal signatures: increased reflection amplitude, delayed pulse arrival, and enhanced waveform broadening in malignant tissue. Hydration-dependent pseudo-Brewster minima provide an additional contrast mechanism by suppressing reflections from low-hydration normal and adipose tissues.
AI.conclusion: The triple-Debye framework offers substantially improved quantitative modeling of THz-tissue interactions, and reflected pulse temporal signatures plus pseudo-Brewster minima emerge as robust hydration-based contrast mechanisms for breast cancer assessment.

title: First Experimental Evidence of Helicon Current Drive
comment: J.B. Lestz, R.I. Pinsker, and B. Van Compernolle contributed equally to this work. 11 pages, 7 figures. Accepted in Physical Review Letters
summary: Helicon current drive is an attractive solution for driving current to sustain steady state tokamak operation in reactor conditions. Dedicated DIII-D experiments have been conducted with a MW-level helicon system and successfully demonstrated core power deposition and current drive with helicon waves launched via a traveling wave antenna. The profile of the measured electron temperature response to helicon power injection is in good agreement with time-dependent integrated modeling that incorporates ray tracing and the effects of thermal transport simultaneously. When the helicon power is injected continuously to drive co-$I_p$ current, the reconstructed safety factor profile flattens significantly faster and sawteeth are triggered earlier than in comparison shots where the helicon is replaced by a comparable amount of electron cyclotron heating. Calculation of the helicon-driven current profile yields a peaked profile in the core, consistent with the observed power deposition profile and in good agreement with ray tracing predictions. Taken together, these experimental results represent strong evidence for the first definitive observation of auxiliary current drive due to helicon waves on any device.

AI.tldr: DIII-D experiments with a MW-level helicon system demonstrate core power deposition and current drive via a traveling wave antenna, providing the first definitive observation of helicon-wave current drive.
AI.motivation: Helicon current drive is attractive for sustaining steady-state tokamak operation in reactor conditions, motivating dedicated experimental demonstration.
AI.method: DIII-D experiments used a MW-level helicon system launching waves via a traveling wave antenna. Electron temperature response was compared with time-dependent integrated modeling (ray tracing + thermal transport). Helicon was compared against comparable electron cyclotron heating, and the driven current profile was reconstructed.
AI.result: Measured electron temperature response agrees well with integrated modeling. With continuous co-Ip helicon injection, the safety factor profile flattens faster and sawteeth trigger earlier than with ECH. The helicon-driven current profile is peaked in the core, consistent with power deposition and ray tracing predictions.
AI.conclusion: These results provide strong evidence for the first definitive observation of auxiliary current drive due to helicon waves on any device.

title: On the parabolic $Φ_3^4$ model for the harmonic oscillator II: global existence and invariant measures
summary: We establish an a priori bound for the dynamical parabolic $Φ_3^4$ model with harmonic potential. This bound yields the global well-posedness of the equation and, via the Krylov-Bogoliubov method, the existence of an invariant measure, shown to be non-Gaussian. The argument builds on the strategy developed by Mourrat and Weber for the periodic $Φ_3^4$ model, with substantial modifications to handle the non-compact geometry of $\mathbb{R}^3$ and the spectral framework imposed by the harmonic oscillator. We further prove that this measure is unique in the small-coupling regime.

AI.tldr: The paper proves a priori bounds for the dynamical parabolic Φ₃⁴ model with harmonic potential, establishing global well-posedness and the existence of a unique non-Gaussian invariant measure in the small-coupling regime.
AI.motivation: The work is motivated by extending the Mourrat-Weber strategy for the periodic Φ₃⁴ model to handle the non-compact geometry of ℝ³ and the spectral framework imposed by the harmonic oscillator.
AI.method: The method establishes an a priori bound, uses the Krylov-Bogoliubov method to construct an invariant measure, and builds on the Mourrat-Weber approach with substantial modifications for non-compact geometry and harmonic oscillator spectral theory.
AI.result: The paper obtains global well-posedness, existence of an invariant measure shown to be non-Gaussian, and uniqueness of this measure in the small-coupling regime.
AI.conclusion: The dynamical parabolic Φ₃⁴ model with harmonic potential is globally well-posed and admits a unique non-Gaussian invariant measure for small coupling, extending previous periodic-setting results to ℝ³.

title: Adaptive local representations for Helmholtz Trefftz discontinuous Galerkin methods
summary: We study the selection and stable realization of local approximation spaces in Trefftz discontinuous Galerkin discretizations of the Helmholtz equation. A scaled Cauchy-trace inner product places plane waves and Fourier-Bessel functions in a common geometry: Fourier-Bessel modes are orthogonal with explicit weights, while the same weights determine the circulant spectrum of an equispaced plane-wave trace Gram matrix. This separates amplitude scaling from genuine trace-rank loss and yields an exact best-approximation identity for mixed plane-wave--Fourier--Bessel spaces. With complex plane-wave angles, the unresolved modal tail is an exponential sequence, so propagating and evanescent components can be identified by the same ESPRIT/variable-projection procedure. We prove exact recovery and a perturbation estimate for the recovered angles and, under the standard PWDG quasi-optimality bound, transfer these perturbations to the DG error. Trace-Riesz orthonormalization is then separated from a graph--Riesz normalization of the assembled operator. Numerical experiments verify the identities, recover sparse ray fields to roundoff, and resolve a propagating-to-evanescent transition without a prescribed critical angle.

AI.tldr: This paper analyzes selection and stable realization of local approximation spaces in Trefftz DG (PWDG) discretizations of the Helmholtz equation, using a scaled Cauchy-trace inner product to unify plane waves and Fourier-Bessel functions, and an ESPRIT-type procedure to recover complex plane-wave angles.
AI.motivation: Local approximation spaces in Trefftz DG for Helmholtz require reliable selection of basis modes and stable numerical realization. Plane waves and Fourier-Bessel modes are usually treated separately, and distinguishing amplitude scaling from genuine trace-rank loss is difficult. The authors aim for a common geometry that makes mode selection and propagating/evanescent identification principled and stable.
AI.method: A scaled Cauchy-trace inner product is introduced that places plane waves and Fourier-Bessel functions in a common framework. Fourier-Bessel modes become orthogonal with explicit weights, and the same weights give the circulant spectrum of the equispaced plane-wave trace Gram matrix. This yields an exact best-approximation identity for mixed plane-wave--Fourier--Bessel spaces. With complex plane-wave angles, the unresolved modal tail is an exponential sequence, enabling identification of propagating and evanescent components via ESPRIT/variable projection. Exact recovery and a perturbation estimate for recovered angles are proved, and perturbations are transferred to DG error under the standard PWDG quasi-optimality bound. Trace-Riesz orthonormalization is separated from graph-Riesz normalization of the assembled operator.
AI.result: The paper proves exact best-approximation identities, exact recovery plus perturbation estimates for the recovered angles, and a transfer of angle perturbations to the DG error under the PWDG quasi-optimality bound. Numerical experiments verify the identities, recover sparse ray fields to roundoff, and resolve a propagating-to-evanescent transition without a prescribed critical angle.
AI.conclusion: The scaled Cauchy-trace inner product provides a unified, stable framework for selecting and realizing PWDG local approximation spaces, cleanly separating amplitude scaling from trace-rank loss and enabling ESPRIT-based recovery of complex plane-wave angles with controlled error propagation to the DG solution.

title: Physics-enriched neural solvers for transient ice-flow simulation
summary: Transient glacier simulations with higher-order ice flow require the repeated solution of a nonlinear problem as the geometry evolves. In the online mode of the Instructed Glacier Model, the velocity field is represented by a neural network whose weights are warm-started from the previous time step and updated with a few optimizer iterations. We show that supplying the network with inexpensive input fields derived from low-order ice-flow balances improves this online solver. Unlike residual-based physics-informed neural networks, which incorporate physics through governing-equation penalties in the loss, our approach leaves the governing energy objective unchanged, adding physical structure through the network inputs. Across three real-world glacier configurations, the enriched solver is markedly more robust to solver settings. On the two alpine cases, it also improves the tuned accuracy--runtime trade-off, reducing surface-velocity errors by factors of two to four at fixed runtime and reaching few-percent relative errors with only $10^4$--$10^5$ trainable parameters, far fewer than comparable raw-input baselines. A 300-year Aletsch simulation then completes in under one minute, and the larger Valais domain in about two minutes, on a single GPU---a budget once reserved for much simpler shallow-ice models. Gains are smaller for the fast marine-terminating glacier, where nonlocal stress coupling favors larger or spectral networks. More broadly, the results suggest that enriching a neural solver's inputs with reduced-order physics can make repeated higher-order solves much cheaper, with no training data and no offline training.

AI.tldr: The Instructed Glacier Model's online neural solver is improved by feeding the network with inexpensive input fields derived from low-order ice-flow balances, boosting robustness and accuracy-runtime trade-off for transient higher-order glacier simulations.
AI.motivation: Transient glacier simulations with higher-order ice flow require repeatedly solving a nonlinear problem as geometry evolves, which is computationally expensive. The online mode of the Instructed Glacier Model approaches this by representing the velocity field with a neural network warm-started from the previous time step, but solver performance can be improved.
AI.method: The authors enrich the network inputs with inexpensive fields derived from low-order ice-flow balances. Unlike residual-based physics-informed neural networks that embed physics via governing-equation penalties in the loss, this approach leaves the governing energy objective unchanged and adds physical structure only through the network inputs.
AI.result: Across three real-world glacier configurations, the enriched solver is more robust to solver settings. On two alpine cases it reduces surface-velocity errors by two to four times at fixed runtime, reaching few-percent relative errors with only 10^4--10^5 trainable parameters, far fewer than raw-input baselines. A 300-year Aletsch simulation completes in under one minute and the Valais domain in about two minutes on a single GPU. Gains are smaller for the fast marine-terminating glacier, where nonlocal stress coupling favors larger or spectral networks.
AI.conclusion: Enriching a neural solver's inputs with reduced-order physics can make repeated higher-order solves much cheaper, with no training data and no offline training. The approach is less effective where nonlocal stress coupling dominates.

title: Nonuniform Hydrodynamic Plasma-Wave Instability in a Gated Electron Channel
summary: We report a theoretical and numerical study of plasma-wave instability in a current-driven InGaAs/GaAs gated electron channel. A finite drain current drives the channel away from a uniform plasma-wave cavity: the carrier density and plasma velocity decrease toward the drain, while the electron drift velocity increases. This current-induced spatial nonuniformity modifies both the propagation time and amplification of plasma waves and becomes increasingly important as the sonic regime is approached. Using a hydrodynamic description combined with the unified charge-control model, we determine the nonuniform steady state and analyze the resulting plasma-wave frequency and instability growth rate. The oscillation frequency is found to be governed by wave propagation through the entire channel rather than by the local drain conditions, leading to a pronounced current-induced frequency reduction that is not captured by a uniform-channel approximation. The instability results from the competition between boundary-induced plasma wave gain and distributed losses due to momentum relaxation and electron viscosity. The finite-viscosity theory shows good quantitative agreement with the simulation data over the subsonic regime and regularizes the singular behavior of the inviscid description near the sonic point. At higher currents, the dynamics become increasingly sensitive to the near-sonic structure and contact boundary conditions, indicating that the eventual suppression of the instability cannot be attributed to bulk hydrodynamics alone.

AI.tldr: Theory and simulation show that a finite drain current makes a current-driven InGaAs/GaAs gated channel spatially nonuniform, strongly modifying plasma-wave frequency and instability in the subsonic regime.
AI.motivation: A uniform-channel approximation ignores that a finite drain current drives the gated electron channel away from a uniform plasma-wave cavity, so the impact of current-induced spatial nonuniformity on plasma-wave propagation and instability needs a proper treatment.
AI.method: Hydrodynamic description combined with the unified charge-control model to compute the nonuniform steady state (carrier density, plasma velocity, drift velocity profiles), then determine plasma-wave frequency and instability growth rate including momentum relaxation and electron viscosity.
AI.result: Oscillation frequency is set by wave propagation through the whole channel rather than local drain conditions, causing a pronounced current-induced frequency reduction missed by uniform-channel models. Instability arises from competition between boundary-induced gain and distributed losses (momentum relaxation, viscosity). Finite-viscosity theory agrees well with simulations in the subsonic regime and regularizes the inviscid singularity near the sonic point.
AI.conclusion: Near the sonic regime the dynamics become highly sensitive to near-sonic structure and contact boundary conditions, so eventual suppression of the instability cannot be explained by bulk hydrodynamics alone.

title: Eigenvalues of the linearized Navier-Stokes operator near locally Couette laminar flows
summary: We consider the spectrum of the Orr-Sommerfeld operator, which is obtained from the linearized Navier-Stokes (LNS) operator near a laminar flow in an infinite two-dimensional channel in the large Reynolds number limit. For a rather general class of laminar flows, which behave locally near the boundary like a Couette flow and are bounded from below (above) by a linear increasing (decreasing) function, we show that there exists an eigenvalue of the LNS operator which coincides, to leading order, with the eigenvalue of LNS near Couette flow, which was formally obtained by Wasow in 1953.

AI.tldr: The paper proves existence of an unstable eigenvalue of the linearized Navier-Stokes (Orr-Sommerfeld) operator in the large Reynolds number limit for a broad class of 2D channel laminar flows, matching Wasow's 1953 formal Couette-flow eigenvalue to leading order.
AI.motivation: Wasow (1953) formally derived an eigenvalue for the LNS operator near Couette flow, but this result lacked rigorous justification. The paper aims to provide a rigorous proof for a general class of laminar flows.
AI.method: Study the spectrum of the Orr-Sommerfeld operator obtained from the linearized Navier-Stokes operator near a laminar flow in an infinite 2D channel in the large Reynolds number limit. Consider a general class of laminar flows that behave locally like Couette flow near the boundary and are bounded by linearly increasing (decreasing) functions.
AI.result: For this general class of laminar flows, the authors show existence of an eigenvalue of the LNS operator coinciding, to leading order, with Wasow's Couette-flow eigenvalue.
AI.conclusion: Wasow's formal 1953 eigenvalue result is rigorously confirmed (to leading order) for a rather general class of laminar flows in the large Reynolds number limit.

title: How to grade the accuracy of the BLAS
summary: Motivated by accelerating machine learning (ML), many computer vendors and chip manufacturers are building accelerators for matrix multiplication, which save time and energy by operating in the lower precisions needed for ML. This has in turn motivated many efforts to use these accelerators to provide faster matrix multiplication implementations with the higher precision required by many other linear algebra applications. Motivated by the large design space of algorithms for approximating higher precision, with significant performance/accuracy tradeoffs, we provide a benchmark to "grade the accuracy" of a matrix multiplication implementation (or the BLAS more generally), ranging from an "A" for attaining the classic floating point error bound, to a "C" for attaining a weaker but still useful bound, that is satisfied by Strassen-like algorithms. We also propose "ungameable" tests that vendors or users can run to verify their promised accuracy, and describe how these different grades impact the accuracy of applications like LU, QR, and Cholesky decomposition. Our test code is publicly available at github.com/Reference-LAPACK/grading-the-BLAS for developers and users, and we also plan to publicly release all our test results.

AI.tldr: The paper proposes a benchmark to "grade the accuracy" of matrix multiplication (and BLAS) implementations, from "A" (classic FP error bound) to "C" (weaker but useful bound satisfied by Strassen-like algorithms), plus "ungameable" tests for verification.
AI.motivation: ML-optimized accelerators run at lower precision, but many linear algebra applications need higher precision. Vendors/users exploit these accelerators for faster high-precision matrix multiplication via approximation algorithms with significant performance/accuracy tradeoffs. There is no standard way to assess the accuracy of such implementations.
AI.method: Define a grading scheme for matrix multiplication/BLAS accuracy: "A" for the classic floating point error bound, "C" for a weaker but still useful bound satisfied by Strassen-like algorithms, with intermediate grades. Propose "ungameable" verification tests and analyze how grades affect LU, QR, and Cholesky decomposition accuracy.
AI.result: A benchmark that grades accuracy of matrix multiplication implementations and "ungameable" tests to verify promised accuracy, with analysis of impact on LU, QR, and Cholesky. Code is publicly available at github.com/Reference-LAPACK/grading-the-BLAS, with plans to release all test results.
AI.conclusion: The grading benchmark and ungameable tests offer developers and users a practical standard to verify and communicate BLAS accuracy, aiding accurate higher-precision computation on ML accelerators.

title: Physically Consistent 2D to 3D Pore Space Synthesis: 1. Dynamic Grain Packing Under Strict Morphology Constraints
summary: The 3D digital reconstruction of multi-scale, heterogeneous porous media is traditionally limited by the resolution boundaries and artifacts of X-ray computed tomography (XCT). This paper introduces a physically consistent 2D to 3D pore space synthesis framework that supersedes conventional geometric shuffling with dynamic Newtonian gravitational deposition using a high-performance rigid-body mechanics engine. To honor strict physical contact mechanics, statistical 2D targets, and morphological constraints, we develop a two-stage dynamic packing pipeline that combines realistic 3D grain shapes with a virtual sub-particle insertion engine. The framework is validated against synthetic and natural core benchmarks. First, we show that our stereological integral equation systematically converts size distributions; bypassing this inversion step induces a systematic 50\% deviation in permeability predictions despite identical total porosities, independently altering flow channel topology. Second, temporary virtual spheres serve as architectural placeholders to stabilize large non-equilibrium dissolution voids, ensuring the reconstructed model satisfies target flow metrics within the prescribed tolerance. Finally, when applied to a fine-grained, weakly consolidated sandstone, the workflow exposes and suppresses systematic XCT artifacts, including phantom internal porosity. Ensembles of two-point correlation functions demonstrate that the hydrodynamically and structurally synthesized digital twins quantitatively exhibit closer structural proximity to the uncorrupted rock geometry than the reference XCT dataset itself. This methodology establishes a scalable foundation for high-fidelity multi-phase rock reconstruction, with potential extensions toward complex amorphous cement phases.

AI.tldr: A physically consistent 2D-to-3D pore space synthesis framework uses Newtonian gravitational deposition with a rigid-body engine to reconstruct multi-scale porous media, outperforming X-ray CT by suppressing artifacts and improving structural fidelity.
AI.motivation: 3D digital reconstruction of multi-scale, heterogeneous porous media is limited by resolution boundaries and artifacts of X-ray computed tomography (XCT), so a method is needed to generate high-fidelity digital twins that bypass these limitations.
AI.method: A two-stage dynamic packing pipeline replaces conventional geometric shuffling with dynamic Newtonian gravitational deposition using a high-performance rigid-body mechanics engine. It combines realistic 3D grain shapes with a virtual sub-particle insertion engine, enforces strict contact mechanics, statistical 2D targets, and morphological constraints, and uses a stereological integral equation to convert size distributions.
AI.result: Skipping the stereological inversion induces ~50% deviation in permeability predictions despite identical total porosities. Temporary virtual spheres stabilize large non-equilibrium dissolution voids, meeting target flow metrics within tolerance. Applied to a fine-grained, weakly consolidated sandstone, the workflow suppresses XCT artifacts such as phantom internal porosity; two-point correlation ensembles show the synthesized twins are structurally closer to the uncorrupted rock than the reference XCT dataset.
AI.conclusion: The methodology provides a scalable foundation for high-fidelity multi-phase rock reconstruction, with potential extensions toward complex amorphous cement phases.

title: A Variational Formulation of the MHD Induction Equation
summary:
We present a variational formulation of the induction equation in magnetohydrodynamics (MHD) based on Gauss's principle of least constraint. The central result is the Euler--Lagrange equation $\mathbf{Z}_B = -
abla h_m$, where $h_m = \mathbf{A}\cdot\mathbf{B}$ is the magnetic helicity density. This reveals that the magnetic helicity gradient $
abla h_m$ acts as the constraint force maintaining the solenoidality of the magnetic field, exactly as the pressure gradient $
abla p$ maintains incompressibility in Taha et al.'s pressure-gradient minimization principle. The magnetic helicity density---which, though gauge-dependent locally, yields a gauge-invariant variational principle---naturally emerges as the Lagrange multiplier enforcing $
abla\cdot\mathbf{B}=0$. At the solution, the field minimizes the norm of the magnetic helicity gradient $\|
abla h_m\|^2$. This establishes a structural analogy: magnetic helicity is to the magnetic field as pressure is to velocity. The variational principle connects to Woltjer's theorem, Taylor relaxation, and the Hamiltonian structure of MHD.

AI.tldr: A variational formulation of the MHD induction equation is derived from Gauss's principle of least constraint, showing the magnetic helicity gradient acts as the constraint force enforcing solenoidality.
AI.motivation: To explain what maintains the solenoidality constraint (div B = 0) in MHD, by analogy with how the pressure gradient maintains incompressibility in a pressure-gradient minimization principle.
AI.method: Gauss's principle of least constraint is applied to the induction equation, yielding an Euler-Lagrange equation Z_B = -∇h_m, with magnetic helicity density h_m = A·B emerging as the Lagrange multiplier for div B = 0.
AI.result: The magnetic helicity gradient ∇h_m acts as the constraint force; the solution minimizes ||∇h_m||². The principle is gauge-invariant despite h_m being locally gauge-dependent.
AI.conclusion: A structural analogy is established: magnetic helicity is to the magnetic field as pressure is to velocity, connecting to Woltjer's theorem, Taylor relaxation, and MHD's Hamiltonian structure.

title: A note on p-harmonic measure
summary: For 1 < p < 2 we obtain the asymptotic optimal decay of the p-harmonic measure of an arc of the unit circle, complementing previous results by Lundström and Vasilis.

AI.tldr: For 1 < p < 2, the asymptotic optimal decay of the p-harmonic measure of an arc of the unit circle is obtained, complementing prior work by Lundström and Vasilis.
AI.motivation: Previous results by Lundström and Vasilis addressed related decay behavior but left the case 1 < p < 2 incomplete. This work fills that gap.
AI.method: The paper establishes the asymptotic optimal decay of the p-harmonic measure of an arc of the unit circle in the range 1 < p < 2.
AI.result: Asymptotically optimal decay for the p-harmonic measure of a circular arc is obtained for 1 < p < 2.
AI.conclusion: The result completes and complements earlier findings by Lundström and Vasilis on p-harmonic measure decay.

title: A spectral-element method for computing many eigenvalues and their asymptotics of the Schrödinger operator with Robin boundary condition
summary: We propose spectral and spectral-element methods for accurately computing many eigenvalues of the Schrödinger operator with Robin boundary condition on simple and complex geometries, respectively. Due to their spectral-type accuracy in approximating those eigenfunctions corresponding to high-index eigenvalues, which are usually highly oscillatory, the proposed approaches have excellent resolution in computing thousands of eigenvalues accurately and efficiently with the resolution property that the number of eigenvalues with reasonable accuracy is proportional to the number of degrees of freedom. Using a standard HPC node with 128 GB of memory, we can obtain numerically more than 5,000 reliable eigenvalues with relative errors below $10^{-8}$ for different complex domains in two dimensions (2D). Based on these computed eigenvalues, we first confirm some theoretical results on the Robin-to-Neumann (RtN) gaps of the Laplacian operator in 2D, which were recently studied by Rudnick \textit{et al.} [\textit{Comm. Math. Phys.} 388 (2021)]. Then we systematically study the RtN gaps of the Schrödinger operator and their convergence rates. Based on our extensive numerical results, we formulate a unified conjecture on the cumulative averages of the RtN gaps of the Schrödinger operator.

AI.tldr: The paper introduces spectral and spectral-element methods for computing many eigenvalues of the Schrödinger operator with Robin boundary conditions on simple and complex geometries, achieving thousands of accurate eigenvalues and studying Robin-to-Neumann gaps.
AI.motivation: Accurately computing many high-index, highly oscillatory eigenvalues of the Schrödinger operator with Robin boundary conditions is challenging; existing approaches may lack resolution and efficiency for thousands of eigenvalues on complex domains.
AI.method: Spectral and spectral-element methods are proposed for simple and complex geometries respectively, exploiting spectral-type accuracy in approximating highly oscillatory eigenfunctions to compute many eigenvalues efficiently.
AI.result: On a standard HPC node with 128 GB memory, more than 5,000 reliable eigenvalues with relative errors below 1e-8 were obtained for various 2D complex domains; number of accurate eigenvalues scales proportionally with degrees of freedom. Theoretical RtN gap results of Rudnick et al. were confirmed, and RtN gaps of the Schrödinger operator and their convergence rates were systematically studied.
AI.conclusion: The methods enable highly accurate and efficient computation of thousands of eigenvalues, and based on extensive numerical results, a unified conjecture on the cumulative averages of the RtN gaps of the Schrödinger operator is formulated.

title: Fundamental Dynamical Units for Physics-Informed Structural Inference from Perturbation Time-Series in Networked Systems
summary: In networked dynamical systems, the parameter of primary mechanistic interest is signed interaction structure. Recovering this structure from perturbation time-series data is a fundamental identification problem, compounded by three coupled obstacles: the combinatorial complexity of interaction architectures, ambiguity of causal attribution under limited interventions, and state-dependent dynamics that confound structural inference. Each obstacle is structural in origin and calls for a structural solution. We address these challenges by adopting a reductionist approach, introducing Fundamental Dynamical Units (FDUs): signed three-node interaction patterns as composable primitives that convert the interaction hypothesis space into a finite, constructive, and tractable representation. We show that local interaction structure determines the perturbation conditions required to disentangle direct from relayed influence, making intervention design a structural consequence of the FDU representation. We embed FDU-regularized structural inference within a physics-informed neural ordinary differential equation (ODE) whose governing-equation constraint transforms structural hypotheses into verifiable dynamical predictions, enabling joint recovery of interaction structure and perturbation-resolved trajectories. Validated on synthetic benchmarks with known ground truth, the framework supports structural commitment, expressed through FDU primitives, motif-prescribed intervention design, and physics-informed learning, as a principled basis for mechanistically interpretable inference in networked dynamical systems.

AI.tldr: This paper introduces Fundamental Dynamical Units (FDUs)—signed three-node interaction patterns as composable primitives—to make interaction-structure recovery from perturbation time-series finite and tractable, embedding FDU-regularized inference in a physics-informed neural ODE for joint recovery of structure and trajectories.
AI.motivation: Recovering signed interaction structure in networked dynamical systems is a fundamental identification problem hindered by three coupled obstacles: combinatorial complexity of interaction architectures, ambiguous causal attribution under limited interventions, and state-dependent dynamics confounding inference. These obstacles are structural in origin and require structural solutions.
AI.method: A reductionist approach using Fundamental Dynamical Units (FDUs): signed three-node interaction patterns as composable primitives that turn the interaction hypothesis space into a finite, constructive, tractable representation. Local structure determines required perturbation conditions, making intervention design a structural consequence of the FDU representation. FDU-regularized structural inference is embedded in a physics-informed neural ODE whose governing-equation constraint turns structural hypotheses into verifiable dynamical predictions.
AI.result: Validated on synthetic benchmarks with known ground truth, the framework enables joint recovery of interaction structure and perturbation-resolved trajectories, supporting structural commitment through FDU primitives, motif-prescribed intervention design, and physics-informed learning.
AI.conclusion: The proposed FDU-based framework offers a principled basis for mechanistically interpretable inference in networked dynamical systems.

title: Optimal regularity for vectorial, higher order and non-minimizing Bernoulli problems
summary: We prove the Lipschitz regularity of solutions for a wide class of generalized Bernoulli free boundary problems, in vectorial, higher order, and non-minimizing settings. Our method does not rely on notions of viscosity solutions or comparison methods, which allows us to reach the optimal regularity for Bernoulli-type problems associated to elliptic operators which do not satisfy any maximum principle, namely the elasticity, biharmonic and Stokes equation. With a similar method we obtain the optimal Lipschitz regularity for stationary, non-minimizing solutions of the standard Bernoulli problem in two dimensions.

AI.tldr: The authors prove optimal Lipschitz regularity for a broad class of generalized Bernoulli free boundary problems, including vectorial, higher-order, and non-minimizing settings, without relying on viscosity solution or comparison techniques.
AI.motivation: Existing regularity results for Bernoulli free boundary problems often depend on viscosity solutions or comparison/maximum principles, which fail for operators such as elasticity, biharmonic, and Stokes equations. There is a need for methods that achieve optimal regularity in these settings.
AI.method: A new approach avoiding viscosity solution notions and comparison methods, applicable to a wide class of generalized Bernoulli problems. Applied also to stationary, non-minimizing solutions of the standard Bernoulli problem in 2D.
AI.result: Optimal Lipschitz regularity is established for Bernoulli-type problems associated with elliptic operators lacking a maximum principle (elasticity, biharmonic, Stokes), and for stationary non-minimizing solutions of the standard Bernoulli problem in two dimensions.
AI.conclusion: The proposed method reaches optimal Lipschitz regularity across vectorial, higher-order, and non-minimizing Bernoulli free boundary problems, notably for operators without a maximum principle, broadening the scope of regularity theory beyond prior viscosity/comparison-based approaches.

title: Early stopping of stochastic variance reduced gradient for linear inverse problems by the discrepancy principle
summary: Stochastic variance reduced gradient (SVRG) is a variant of stochastic gradient descent and is a promising iterative method for solving large-scale inverse problems. Nevertheless, the development of theoretically grounded a posteriori stopping rules for SVRG remains an open challenge. In this work, we provide a convergence analysis of SVRG equipped with the discrepancy principle, the most well-known a posteriori stopping rule, for solving a class of linear inverse problems in Hilbert spaces. We establish the regularizing property of SVRG, and moreover, under suitable source conditions, we derive convergence rates of SVRG iterates. To the best of our knowledge, these are the first convergence rate results of any stochastic iterative method for inverse problems under the a posteriori stopping rule. The theoretical findings are supported by numerical experiments.

AI.tldr: This work analyzes SVRG for linear inverse problems in Hilbert spaces, establishing its regularizing property and, for the first time, convergence rates of a stochastic iterative method under the a posteriori discrepancy principle stopping rule.
AI.motivation: SVRG is promising for large-scale inverse problems, but theoretically grounded a posteriori stopping rules are still lacking. The discrepancy principle is the most well-known such rule, yet its use with SVRG has not been justified theoretically.
AI.method: The authors perform a convergence analysis of SVRG equipped with the discrepancy principle for a class of linear inverse problems in Hilbert spaces, proving the regularizing property and deriving convergence rates under suitable source conditions.
AI.result: SVRG is shown to be a regularizing method, and convergence rates of SVRG iterates are obtained under source conditions. These are claimed to be the first convergence rate results for any stochastic iterative method for inverse problems under an a posteriori stopping rule. Numerical experiments support the theory.
AI.conclusion: The study provides theoretical grounding for the discrepancy principle as a stopping rule for SVRG, marking the first convergence rate analysis of a stochastic iterative method for inverse problems under a posteriori stopping.

title: Diagonal Pair Coulomb Density Matrix on a Sphere: a numerical study
summary: We tabulate, on the diagonal, the $n$th power of the primitive approximation for the pair Coulomb density matrix on a sphere, with up to $n=5$, and we discuss its behavior at particles contact as $n$ grows. Our results show that even on a curved surface quantum statistical physics is fundamentally different from its classical counterpart. If in the latter one needs to artificially introduce a regularization of the divergent attractive Coulomb potential preventing particles contact, for example with a hard core, in the former this is not necessary.

AI.tldr: The paper computes diagonal elements of the nth power of the primitive approximation for the pair Coulomb density matrix on a sphere up to n=5, showing that quantum statistical physics on a curved surface avoids the need for artificial regularization of the attractive Coulomb potential.
AI.motivation: Classical treatments of the attractive Coulomb potential require artificial regularization (e.g., a hard core) to prevent particles from contacting. The authors investigate whether this necessity persists in the quantum statistical setting on a curved surface.
AI.method: They tabulate the diagonal elements of the nth power of the primitive approximation for the pair Coulomb density matrix on a sphere, up to n=5, and analyze its behavior at particle contact as n grows.
AI.result: The primitive approximation's diagonal behavior at contact is examined as n increases, demonstrating that the quantum statistical treatment on a curved surface diverges from the classical one.
AI.conclusion: Even on a curved surface, quantum statistical physics is fundamentally different from its classical counterpart: no artificial regularization of the attractive Coulomb potential is needed to prevent particle contact.

title: Doubling inequalities and propagation of smallness for Schrödinger equations with singular potentials
summary:
We study quantitative unique continuation for solutions of the Schrö\-din\-ger equation with complex-valued singular potentials \(V\in L^t\), \(t>d/2\). We obtain a family of scale-invariant \(L^p\to L^q\) Carleman inequalities for the Laplacian and use them to prove the doubling inequalities with explicit dependence on the
  \(L^t\)-norm of the potential. These estimates are combined with multiscale arguments to obtain propagation of smallness from arbitrary measurable sets of positive measure. As an application of the main results, we prove an upper bound for the BMO norm for the logarithms of Dirichlet-Laplace eigenfunctions in simply connected planar Lipschitz domains.

AI.tldr: The paper develops scale-invariant Carleman inequalities for the Laplacian to prove quantitative unique continuation for Schrödinger equations with complex-valued singular potentials, yielding doubling inequalities and propagation of smallness, with applications to BMO bounds for eigenfunction logarithms.
AI.motivation: Quantitative unique continuation for Schrödinger equations with complex-valued singular potentials in L^t (t>d/2) is a challenging problem, and existing techniques often lack explicit dependence on potential norms or scale-invariant estimates. The authors aim to establish robust quantitative results (doubling inequalities, propagation of smallness) that are both scale-invariant and applicable to singular potentials.
AI.method: The authors prove a family of scale-invariant L^p → L^q Carleman inequalities for the Laplacian, then use them to derive doubling inequalities with explicit dependence on the L^t-norm of the potential. These are combined with multiscale arguments to obtain propagation of smallness from arbitrary measurable sets of positive measure.
AI.result: The main results include: scale-invariant Carleman inequalities for the Laplacian; doubling inequalities with explicit L^t-norm dependence; propagation of smallness from arbitrary measurable sets of positive measure; and, as an application, an upper bound for the BMO norm of the logarithms of Dirichlet-Laplace eigenfunctions in simply connected planar Lipschitz domains.
AI.conclusion: The paper establishes a general quantitative unique continuation framework for Schrödinger operators with complex-valued singular potentials, with explicit scale-invariant estimates and applications to eigenfunction regularity (BMO bounds) in planar Lipschitz domains.

title: 3D Computational Modeling of the Vascular Heat-Sink Effect in Microwave Ablation of Tumors Close to the Aorta
summary: Microwave ablation (MWA) is a percutaneous ablation that induces thermal necrosis by generating localized high-temperature regions within tumor tissue. However, when a tumor is located close to a large vessel such as the aorta, blood flow continuously removes heat from the ablation zone. This phenomenon causes the vascular heat-sink effect and thereby increases the risk of incomplete ablation. This study constructs an ANSYS-based numerical framework to investigate the heat-sink effect during MWA of tumors located close to the aorta. The computational model consists of the tumor, surrounding tissue, vessel wall, blood flow domain, and microwave antenna. Microwave-induced heating was represented by an equivalent heat source mapped from the High-Frequency Structure Simulator (HFSS)-derived volume loss density, rather than by direct electromagnetic-thermal coupling within the thermal-fluid solver. Two parametric studies were performed to quantify the heat-sink effect. First, the tumor-aorta distance was varied at D = 0 mm, 4 mm, and 8.5 mm to assess how vessel proximity affects temperature elevation and ablation zone formation. Second, at each tumor-aorta distance, three blood-flow conditions were compared: no blood, stagnant blood V = 0 m/s, and normal aortic blood flow V=0.65 m/s. This comparison enabled the heat-sink effect of blood flow to be independently evaluated. The results highlight the clinical need for simulation-based treatment planning in patients with tumors located close to major vessels.

AI.tldr: An ANSYS-based numerical framework simulates the vascular heat-sink effect during microwave ablation of tumors near the aorta, showing that vessel proximity and blood flow reduce ablation efficacy.
AI.motivation: MWA induces thermal necrosis, but tumors near large vessels like the aorta suffer a vascular heat-sink effect: flowing blood continuously removes heat from the ablation zone, increasing the risk of incomplete ablation. This study aims to quantify this effect to support treatment planning.
AI.method: An ANSYS-based thermal-fluid model was built including tumor, surrounding tissue, vessel wall, blood flow domain, and microwave antenna. Heating was applied as an equivalent heat source derived from HFSS volume loss density instead of direct EM-thermal coupling. Two parametric studies were run: (1) tumor-aorta distance D = 0, 4, 8.5 mm; (2) three blood-flow conditions (no blood, stagnant V=0 m/s, normal V=0.65 m/s) at each distance.
AI.result: Vessel proximity and blood flow both affected temperature elevation and ablation zone formation. The comparison across blood-flow conditions allowed the heat-sink effect to be evaluated independently from distance effects.
AI.conclusion: The findings highlight the clinical need for simulation-based treatment planning in patients with tumors located close to major vessels.

title: Functionalization-Driven Charge Redistribution Enabling Ultra-High-Capacity V2B MBene Anode for Li/Na ion batteries: A First-Principles study
summary: Amid increasing global demand for clean, sustainable energy, the search for novel electrode materials has emerged as a crucial link to advancing future energy storage technologies. Here, we explored the potential of N-functionalized 2D MBene V2BN2 as anode materials for Li- and Na-ion batteries using first-principles calculations. Phonon dispersion and ab initio molecular dynamics calculations were employed to assess the dynamic and thermal stability of the material. The intrinsic metallic properties of V2BN2 were revealed through electronic band structures and density of states analyses. Importantly, Bader charge analysis demonstrates substantial charge redistribution upon Li/Na adsorption, leading to stronger ion-substrate interactions compared to the pristine counterpart. This redistribution plays a decisive role in enhancing Li/Na ion adsorption and stabilizing ion accommodation. Furthermore, owing to favorable multilayer adsorption of Li and Na ions, V2BN2 exhibited high theoretical specific capacities of 1524 and 762 mAh/g, as well as low open circuit voltages of 0.73 and 0.23 V for Li and Na, respectively. In addition, the energy barriers were calculated to be 0.49 and 0.29 eV for Li- and Na-ion transport, respectively, indicating rapid ion transport and excellent rate capability. These results indicate that V2BN2 holds significant potential as an anode material for next-generation rechargeable ion batteries.

AI.tldr: First-principles study of N-functionalized 2D MBene V2BN2 as a promising anode for Li- and Na-ion batteries with high capacity and fast ion transport.
AI.motivation: Increasing global demand for clean, sustainable energy drives the search for novel electrode materials for advanced energy storage.
AI.method: First-principles calculations; phonon dispersion and ab initio molecular dynamics for stability; band structure and density of states for metallicity; Bader charge analysis for ion-substrate interactions; evaluation of adsorption, specific capacity, open circuit voltage, and diffusion barriers.
AI.result: V2BN2 is dynamically/thermally stable and intrinsically metallic. Strong charge redistribution enhances Li/Na adsorption. High specific capacities (1524 mAh/g for Li, 762 mAh/g for Na), low OCVs (0.73 V and 0.23 V), and low diffusion barriers (0.49 eV for Li, 0.29 eV for Na).
AI.conclusion: V2BN2 shows significant potential as an anode material for next-generation rechargeable ion batteries.

title: Sobolev Regularity in Mixed and Isotropic Scales for Vector Fields on the Torus
summary:
We study regularity, existence, and uniqueness of solutions to vector fields on the two-dimensional torus in Sobolev spaces of dominating mixed smoothness, which measure regularity separately in the two variables.
  For constant-coefficient vector fields, we obtain families of mixed smoothness estimates describing how the gain or loss of regularity can be distributed between the two variables. In the nonreal case, a gain of one derivative can be distributed between the two directions, whereas for real irrational coefficients the loss is governed by the irrationality measure of the coefficient. We also establish sharpness below the corresponding arithmetic threshold and describe the rational and Liouville obstructions.
  For real-valued variable coefficients, direct estimates for the periodic Fourier-mode equations yield mixed smoothness regularity results and their isotropic and classical consequences. We then use a periodic conjugation to the averaged constant-coefficient normal form. Although this conjugation introduces an additional loss in the mixed smoothness scale, it preserves isotropic Sobolev orders and therefore transfers the sharp constant-coefficient isotropic theory to the variable-coefficient setting. In the nonresonant regimes, we also obtain existence and uniqueness under the natural zero-mean compatibility condition.

AI.tldr: The paper studies regularity, existence, and uniqueness for vector fields on the 2D torus in Sobolev spaces of dominating mixed smoothness, with separate regularity control in each variable, covering constant and variable coefficients.
AI.motivation: Classical isotropic Sobolev theory hides how regularity gains/losses distribute between variables. Mixed smoothness measures regularity separately in each variable, so the authors aim to refine regularity statements for transport/vector-field equations and capture arithmetic effects of coefficients.
AI.method: For constant coefficients, they derive families of mixed smoothness estimates; for nonreal coefficients a one-derivative gain is distributable across directions, while real irrational coefficients yield loss governed by the irrationality measure. Sharpness is shown below the arithmetic threshold via rational and Liouville obstructions. For real variable coefficients, they estimate periodic Fourier-mode equations directly, then conjugate to an averaged constant-coefficient normal form, which lifts mixed-scale loss but preserves isotropic orders.
AI.result: Mixed smoothness estimates are obtained for constant-coefficient vector fields with explicit gain/loss distribution, sharpness below the arithmetic threshold, and described rational/Liouville obstructions. For variable coefficients, direct Fourier-mode estimates give mixed-smoothness results and isotropic/classical consequences; conjugation transfers sharp isotropic theory to the variable setting; existence and uniqueness follow under zero-mean compatibility in nonresonant regimes.
AI.conclusion: Dominating mixed smoothness refines regularity theory for 2D torus vector fields, capturing arithmetic and direction-dependent effects. A normal-form conjugation preserves isotropic orders, enabling transfer of sharp constant-coefficient results to variable coefficients and yielding existence/uniqueness in nonresonant regimes.

title: A Structural Relationship Between Crouzeix-Raviart Immersed Finite Elements for Elliptic and Stokes Interface Problems
summary: In this paper, we study the structural relationship between immersed finite element (IFE) spaces for scalar elliptic and Stokes interface problems on unfitted meshes. Although IFE methods have been widely developed for individual partial differential equation models, the algebraic connection between scalar and vector IFE spaces has not been systematically explored. We establish a precise unisolvence relationship between the immersed Crouzeix-Raviart (CR) element for elliptic interface problems and the immersed CR-$P_0$ element for Stokes interface problems in both gradient and stress formulations. By analyzing the block structure of the local IFE matrices, we show that the determinant of the Stokes IFE matrix factorizes in terms of the determinant of the corresponding elliptic IFE matrix. This factorization reveals an intrinsic algebraic link between the two classes of immersed elements and explains the unisolvence of the Stokes IFE spaces through the scalar elliptic case. The same result extends naturally to three dimensions and significantly simplifies the corresponding analysis. Numerical experiments confirm optimal convergence rates for both velocity and pressure in three-dimensional Stokes interface problems.

AI.tldr: This paper establishes an algebraic unisolvence relationship between immersed finite element (IFE) spaces for scalar elliptic and Stokes interface problems on unfitted meshes, showing the Stokes IFE matrix determinant factorizes via the elliptic IFE matrix determinant.
AI.motivation: IFE methods have been developed for individual PDE models, but the algebraic connection between scalar and vector IFE spaces has not been systematically explored.
AI.method: The authors analyze the block structure of local IFE matrices to relate the immersed CR element (elliptic) with the immersed CR-$P_0$ element (Stokes) in gradient and stress formulations, deriving a determinant factorization. The result is extended to 3D.
AI.result: The Stokes IFE matrix determinant factorizes in terms of the elliptic IFE matrix determinant, revealing an intrinsic algebraic link and explaining Stokes IFE unisolvence via the scalar case; this simplifies 3D analysis. Numerical experiments confirm optimal convergence rates for velocity and pressure in 3D Stokes interface problems.
AI.conclusion: An intrinsic algebraic link exists between scalar and vector immersed elements, providing a unified way to establish unisolvence and simplifying both 2D and 3D analysis.

title: Error-Rate Reduction in LDPC Decoding via Bit-Aligned Temporal Reinforcement in Parallel Probabilistic-Bit Dynamics
summary: Probabilistic bits (p-bits) provide a physical and algorithmic primitive for stochastic inference, but highly parallel updates can alter their collective dynamics. We study the decoding of random-regular (3, 6) low-density parity-check (LDPC) codes using Jacobi-type p-bit annealing with stochastic partial activation. An additive response-path rule stores each bit's saturated response and reuses it before stochastic readout. High-statistics simulations with independent parameter optimization for each method show pooled bit-error-rate reductions of 33.5%, 74.8%, and 81.8% relative to memoryless probabilistic simulated annealing (pSA) for representative codes of block lengths 96, 192, and 288, respectively. Static gain, normalized averaging, response shuffling, and same-bit binary-state feedback with only its coefficient tuned under the same nonmemory parameters do not reproduce the full saturated-response benefit. Trajectory analysis links the improvement to acquisition of the channel-consistent valid-codeword basin and enhanced post-acquisition stability; the acquisition advantage persists from random and channel-hard-decision starts under the tested conditions. Across all 30 independent code realizations, fixed additive parameter-and-readout packages achieve lower bit- and frame-error rates than separately optimized pSA-specific packages, with neither package retuned for individual codes. These results show that the computational effect of temporal state depends on the retained quantity and its reinjection into stochastic dynamics.

AI.tldr: A p-bit Jacobi-type annealing decoder with a saturated-response memory rule improves LDPC decoding error rates substantially over memoryless pSA.
AI.motivation: Probabilistic bits offer a physical/algorithmic primitive for stochastic inference, but highly parallel updates can change their collective dynamics, motivating study of how temporal state retention affects decoding.
AI.method: Jacobi-type p-bit annealing with stochastic partial activation for random-regular (3,6) LDPC codes, using an additive response-path rule that stores each bit's saturated response and reuses it before stochastic readout; high-statistics simulations with independent parameter optimization per method, plus trajectory analysis and tests of alternative memory schemes.
AI.result: Pooled bit-error-rate reductions of 33.5%, 74.8%, and 81.8% versus memoryless pSA for block lengths 96, 192, 288. Static gain, normalized averaging, response shuffling, and same-bit binary-state feedback do not reproduce the benefit. Over 30 code realizations, fixed additive packages outperform separately optimized pSA-specific packages.
AI.conclusion: The computational effect of temporal state depends on the retained quantity and how it is reinjected into stochastic dynamics; saturated-response memory helps acquire the valid-codeword basin and stabilizes post-acquisition.

title: Multi-Spectral QPAT with Frequency Averaged Measurements
summary: We study some inverse problems in a frequency-averaged model for quantitative photoacoustic tomography, in which the optical parameters are modeled by a finite number of spectral functions and spatial coefficients, and the measurements are given by internal observables averaged over a spectral bandwidth. Using multiple measurements generated by suitable complex geometrical optics solutions, we establish uniqueness and Lipschitz-type stability for the associated linearized inverse problem for diffusion and absorption recovery. This linearized stability further yields local Hölder-type stability for the nonlinear inverse problem via an abstract linear-to-nonlinear argument.

AI.tldr: The paper studies inverse problems in a frequency-averaged model for quantitative photoacoustic tomography, establishing uniqueness and stability results for recovering optical (diffusion and absorption) parameters that are modeled as separable spectral-spatial functions.
AI.motivation: In quantitative photoacoustic tomography, optical parameters typically depend on Both wavelength (spectral) and space. Modeling these as finite sums of spectral functions and spatial coefficients with spectrally-averaged internal measurements captures realistic multi-spectral data while remaining tractable. The goal is to determine whether diffusion and absorption can be uniquely and stably recovered in this setting.
AI.method: The authors use multiple measurements generated by suitably constructed complex geometrical optics (CGO) solutions. They linearize the inverse problem and analyze the associated linearized problem, proving uniqueness and Lipschitz-type stability for diffusion and absorption recovery.
AI.result: Uniqueness and Lipschitz-type stability are established for the linearized inverse problem of diffusion and absorption recovery. This linearized stability then yields local Hölder-type stability for the original nonlinear inverse problem through an abstract linear-to-nonlinear argument.
AI.conclusion: The work provides rigorous uniqueness and stability guarantees for a frequency-averaged quantitative photoacoustic tomography model, extending linearized stability to local Hölder stability for the nonlinear problem.

title: Sharp Error Estimates for a Fully Discrete Finite Element Method for Semilinear SPDEs with Multiplicative Noise and Nonsmooth Initial Data
summary: This article establishes sharp strong error estimates for the fully discrete approximation of semilinear parabolic stochastic partial differential equations (SPDEs) driven by multiplicative noise and subject to nonsmooth initial data. The spatial discretization is based on a standard finite element method, coupled with the linearly implicit Euler scheme in time. By mapping the diffusion operator into negative fractional spaces, our framework accommodates both trace-class and space-time white noise. For nonsmooth initial data, by decoupling the noise regularity parameter $β\in (0,2)$ from the initial data regularity parameter $μ\in (0,2]$, we derive sharp regularity estimates that isolate the exact loss of initial regularity into an integrable temporal singularity. Furthermore, we establish sharp strong convergence rates of $O(h^{β-\varepsilon} + k^{\frac{1}{2}\min\{β-\varepsilon, 1\}})$ for $\varepsilon>0$ away from $t = 0$. Finally, we consider physically relevant stochastic models, such as the modified Langmuir fractional surface coverage model and the parabolic Anderson model, in our numerical experiments to confirm the theoretical convergence rates.

AI.tldr: The paper proves sharp strong error estimates for fully discrete finite element approximations of semilinear parabolic SPDEs with multiplicative noise and nonsmooth initial data, using a linearly implicit Euler scheme in time.
AI.motivation: Existing error analyses for numerical approximations of semilinear parabolic SPDEs often assume smooth initial data or fail to isolate how nonsmooth initial data interacts with noise regularity. This work aims to provide sharp error estimates that decouple the noise regularity from the initial data regularity.
AI.method: Spatial discretization via standard finite element method, temporal discretization via linearly implicit Euler scheme. The diffusion operator is mapped into negative fractional spaces to handle both trace-class and space-time white noise. Noise regularity parameter β ∈ (0,2) is decoupled from initial data regularity parameter μ ∈ (0,2].
AI.result: Sharp regularity estimates isolating the loss of initial regularity as an integrable temporal singularity, and sharp strong convergence rates O(h^{β−ε} + k^{½ min{β−ε,1}}) for ε>0 away from t=0. Numerical experiments on the modified Langmuir fractional surface coverage model and the parabolic Anderson model confirm the theoretical rates.
AI.conclusion: The framework yields sharp strong convergence rates for fully discrete approximations of semilinear parabolic SPDEs under nonsmooth initial data and general multiplicative noise, validated by physically relevant stochastic models.

title: Diversifying time evolution of matrix product states using BUGs
summary: Time evolution of tensor-network states is a central tool for studying nonequilibrium dynamics in strongly correlated quantum systems. In the past decade, using the time-dependent variational principle (TDVP) discretized by projector-splitting has become the gold standard for evolving matrix product states (MPS) with long-range Hamiltonians. More recently, a conceptually different class of discretizations of the TDVP, the class of Basis Update and Galerkin (BUG) integrators, has been developed within the framework of dynamical low-rank approximation, offering an alternative, more flexible approach. In this work, we formulate two BUG integrators explicitly for MPS. The BUG integrators result in "single-site" MPS integrators that are robust with respect to small singular values, avoid backward-in-time substeps, and naturally allow for the adaptive choice of bond dimensions. We consider the augmented BUG integrator of first order and the midpoint BUG integrator of second order and clarify their relation to the projector-splitting discretization of the TDVP. Using representative models of strongly correlated quantum systems, like the XY spin model with long-range interaction and two-dimensional lattice models of fermions and spins of various lengths, we perform a systematic numerical comparison between BUG and projector-splitting time discretizations of the continuous-time TDVP, focusing on scalability, numerical complexity, and accuracy.
